summary: Extends DHCP so the server can start a reconfiguration of a client that already has a lease, for example to give it a new address or new settings. Normally only the client starts these exchanges. It is a standards-track document.

eli5.summary: Usually a computer has to knock on the door to ask for new settings. This lets the helper who hands out settings tap the computer on the shoulder and say that something changed.

questions: how can a dhcp server push new settings to a client
subtitle: Lets a DHCP server tell one client to renew its lease now, instead of waiting to be asked.

tldr.problem: In plain DHCP only the client starts an exchange, so a server cannot make a host pick up a new address or new settings before its lease runs out.
tldr.mechanism: The server sends a unicast FORCERENEW message (DHCP message type 9). The client moves to the RENEW state and renews its lease the normal way, and a NAK can push it back to a full DISCOVER.
tldr.outcome: FORCERENEW MUST be authenticated with the DHCP authentication procedures, and flooding a client with bogus messages is a denial of service risk. RFC 6704 later updated this RFC.

today: RFC 3203 is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 6704. It was written to be used together with the DHCP authentication procedures of RFC 3118.

sections.title: Reconfiguring a Host from the Server
sections.content:
This RFC defines extensions to DHCP that allow dynamic reconfiguration of a single host, triggered by the DHCP server. The change might be a new IP address, new local configuration parameters, or both. It does this by adding a unicast FORCERENEW message that forces the client into the RENEW state. The RFC also says how hosts that use the DHCP INFORM message should behave.

The key words MUST, SHOULD and so on are used as in RFC 2119.
sections.eli5: Normally you have to ask the lunch lady for a new tray. Here the lunch lady can walk over and tell one kid to come and ask again.

sections.title: Force Renew Procedures
sections.content:
The server sends a unicast FORCERENEW to the client. On receipt, the client changes to the RENEW state and renews its lease with normal DHCP procedures. If the server wants the client to take a new address, it answers the client's DHCP REQUEST with a DHCP NAK. The client then goes back to the init state and broadcasts a DHCP DISCOVER, and the server can reply with an OFFER carrying the new address.

If the FORCERENEW is lost, the server sees no REQUEST from the client. It should then retransmit using an exponential backoff, choosing a delay that suits the bandwidth between server and client, and it should limit the number of retransmissions.

A multicast FORCERENEW should be silently discarded by the client. A client that got its address some other way (manual configuration, for example) and only uses INFORM to get other parameters should answer a unicast FORCERENEW with a new INFORM. It should not override manually configured parameters.

Reconfiguring a client this way can interrupt active sessions, so the procedures should be used in controlled circumstances.
sections.eli5: The helper taps one computer on the shoulder, and the computer asks again for its settings. If the helper wants it to change address, the helper says no to the old one, and the computer starts over.

sections.title: Example Uses and Rationale
sections.content:
The RFC gives three example uses. Embedded clients such as home gateways can be told to contact the server before their lease expires, which allows service changes or interruptions. In a hotel, the server can hand out limited-use addresses first and later trigger a new initialization so the guest gets a globally routed address. Under tightly controlled conditions, FORCERENEW can renumber whole subnets, client by client.

The stated advantages are that no new states are needed in the client, which minimizes code changes, and that lease renewal can be driven by the server, which can optimize network usage or server load.
sections.eli5: A hotel gives you a basic pass at first. Later it can ask you to come back to the desk to get a better one.

sections.title: Message Layout and the Extended State Diagram
sections.content:
FORCERENEW uses the normal DHCP message layout. The only change is a new value for DHCP option 53 (DHCP message type): DHCPFORCERENEW, value 9. IANA is asked to record that value.

The extended state diagram in the RFC adds one arrow to the DHCP client's states. A client in the Bound state can move to Renew either when timer T1 expires or on receiving the DHCPFORCERENEW message, and the rest of the diagram is unchanged.
sections.eli5: It is the same envelope as always, with a new sticker on it that says: please renew.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
FORCERENEW could be used to snoop on and spoof traffic in some network environments. So the message MUST be authenticated using the procedures in RFC 3118, and messages that fail authentication should be silently discarded by the client.

The mechanism is still open to a denial of service attack: a flood of bogus FORCERENEW messages can make a client spend so much effort on authentication checks that the device is overwhelmed.
sections.eli5: Only a real helper should be allowed to tap you on the shoulder. But if a crowd of fakes taps you all day, you get too tired to do anything else.
